newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy leftist leader appeals to Marxists.
newsitem.headline: Italy leftist leader appeals to Marxists.

text.p: The leader of the largest party in Italy's governing coalition appealed on Tuesday to the hard-left Communist Refoundation to act responsibly in the wake of first round local elections which strengthened the Marxists' hand.
In the mayoral elections, candidates backed by Prime Minster Romano Prodi's Olive Tree coalition trailed behind those of the centre-right in the big prize cities of Milan and Turin.

In those cities and in several other smaller municipalities the centre-left may need Communist Refoundation's help to beat the centre-right leaders in the May 11 run-offs and party leader Fausto Bertinotti indicated the political price could be high.
"Given that we got so many votes, this will give more importance to both our social spending and structural reform position," he said.
Refoundation did particularly well in elections for provincial presidents where it won some 12 percent of the vote compared to 9.2 percent in provincial elections in 1993.
"Bertinotti has to understand the responsibilty of his power," Massimo D'Alema, head of the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), told Italian radio.
"I think getting votes means assuming one's responsiblity. At least we think so and I hope this is true also for Communist Refoundation," said D'Alema, whose PDS is the largest coalition partner.
Prodi relies on Communist Refoundation for his majority in the lower house and Bertinotti has used his position to wrest concessions on legislation, particularly on social spending.
Commentators and opposition parties said the weekend elections would most likely encourage Bertinotti to raise the price of his party's support.

"These results could have very negative implications in the short-term because what we have is a government that is no longer a government of the centre-left but a government of the left," said opposition leader Silvio Berlusconi.
"The weight of Communist Refoundation has become predominant and so (Communist Refoundation's) policies will become predominant," he told Italian radio in an interview.
Bertinotti agreed with Berlusconi. "The possibility of shifting the axis of the government more to the left is closer after the elections," he said.

Most of the elections in more than 100 cities and towns with a population of more than 15,000 will have to go to a run-off on May 11. Run-offs will not be held in some 1,000 smaller towns and villages.

Final results from the first round mayoral races showed D'Alema's PDS with the largest share of the vote, with 17.0 percent. Refoundation was the second-largest among the leftist parties, with some 7.9 percent.
The centre-left's poor showing in Milan and Turin galvanised Berlusconi to declare war on the government. He indicated he would not make deals to help enact measures to cut spending.
"We will not give one more vote to this government," he said in Tuesday's radio interview.
Berlusconi, who was prime minister in 1994, had said previously he would be willing to back Prodi on economic policy if the government ditched Refoundation as an ally.

Berlusconi was apparently responding to comments in Washington by Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini that cuts in social spending, including on pensions, had to be made even if that meant breaking Prodi's parliamentary majority.

Dini, a former central banker who heads the small, centrist Italian Renewal party, has had a series of rows with Bertinotti over how to cut costs to ensure Italy is in the first wave of countries adopting the single European currency.
Berlusconi appealed to Dini to take his party out of the coalition, saying it was no longer faithful to the promises it made to centrist voters in the 1996 general elections.
